Daniel’s framing usefully highlights a real function of capital markets: *prices* can update faster than *physical retooling*, and that can hasten “creative destruction” in the Schumpeterian sense ([Schumpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Schumpeter)). But he quietly slides from “a stock price drops” to “assets get emptied or repurposed,” and that’s the key blind spot. Equity prices reallocate *claims* to future cash flows; they do not by themselves reallocate machines, workers, supply chains, or regulatory permissions. Even in public markets, the transmission from valuation to real reorganization is mediated by mechanisms with their own frictions—credit constraints, covenants, bankruptcy law, worker mobility, planning lags, and political resistance. A collapsing market cap can make financing more expensive and invite activism or takeover, but it can also trap a firm in a “zombie” state if debt overhang prevents fresh investment, or it can induce fire-sale dynamics that destroy organizational capital rather than smoothly “repurpose” it. In short: finance can *signal* and *discipline* quickly; whether it *accelerates structural change* depends on governance and institutional plumbing, not just prediction.

The stronger problem is Daniel’s categorical claim that finance “only ever moves resources among places, never through time.” In mainstream intertemporal economics, lending/borrowing and insurance are precisely *time trades*: they shift purchasing power and risk exposure across dates (consumption smoothing, investment front-loading), even if the physical goods are produced and consumed in their own time. Irving Fisher’s classic setup is literally about exchanging present for future consumption via interest rates ([Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Interest)). One can rescue Daniel’s point by rephrasing: finance does not move *physical goods backward in time*; it reallocates *rights, obligations, and risk* across time, which then changes what gets built now. But as written, the “never through time” line reads less like a clarifying correction and more like an unnecessary provocation—and it undermines his own argument, because the acceleration he describes (building new capacity sooner, shrinking old capacity sooner) often relies on intertemporal contracting: raising capital today against uncertain payoffs tomorrow.

Finally, Daniel assumes “equilibrium” as the destination and treats deduction about the future as largely aggregative and stabilizing. That neglects the Keynesian point that markets can be a coordination device for *expectations about expectations*, not just forecasts about fundamentals, which can amplify cascades and delay structural adjustment rather than speed it ([Keynes, beauty contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian_beauty_contest)). If the post’s core thesis is that finance accelerates structural change, the missing nuance is that it can also accelerate *wrong* structural change—and the difference hinges less on “speed” than on incentives, information quality, and the institutions that convert prices into real reallocation.
